implementation_notes: The class structure collapses into two stdlib idioms: asyncio.start_server (or loop.create_server) is the acceptor—it binds, listens and invokes the per-connection callback with (reader, writer); asyncio.open_connection/create_connection is the connector; Server.serve_forever() drives acceptance. If start_serving=False is selected, await Server.start_serving() explicitly before serving. Blocking socketserver.ThreadingTCPServer is the manual fallback.
code_sketch:
async def main():
    server = await asyncio.start_server(handle_session, host, 8080, start_serving=False)
    await server.start_serving()
    async with server:
        await server.serve_forever()
# connector: reader, writer = await asyncio.open_connection(host, 8080)
pitfalls: The (reader, writer) pair must be closed explicitly; abandoned transports leak descriptors.
A synchronous blocking call inside a connection coroutine stalls the whole loop; use await or run in an executor.
start_server defaults to start_serving=True; when using start_serving=False, call await server.start_serving()—there is no synchronous server.start() API.
asyncio.open_connection() raises ConnectionRefusedError if the server is not yet listening; add a bounded retry/backoff in production connectors.
The default backlog is 100; under heavy load increase it to match expected concurrency.
